intro: In Britain, talking about the weather is almost a national sport: it is the easiest way to start a conversation. In this lesson you learn to describe the weather (It’s sunny, It’s raining), talk about temperatures and seasons, understand a forecast and react naturally (Lovely day, isn’t it?).
objectifs: Describe the weather with “It’s + adjective” and “It’s + -ing verb”.
Tell the noun, the adjective and the verb apart: rain / rainy / it’s raining.
Talk about temperatures and seasons, and understand a weather forecast.
Use the weather to make small talk.

texte: For the weather, English always uses the subject “it”: “It’s cold.” “It’s raining.” “It was windy yesterday.”
To ask: “What’s the weather like?” or “What’s the weather like in Douala today?” Careful: here “like” doesn’t mean “enjoy”; it means “how is it / describe it”.
“weather” is uncountable: “nice weather”, “bad weather”, never “a nice weather”. Don’t confuse it with “time” (hours, minutes) or with “whether” (= if), which sounds the same.
exemples: What’s the weather like today? — It’s sunny and warm.
It was very cold in Montreal last week.
We had lovely weather on holiday.

texte: Many weather words have three forms: the noun (“rain”, “sun”, “wind”), the adjective with -y (“rainy”, “sunny”, “windy”) and sometimes a verb (“to rain”, “to snow”).
We say “It’s sunny / cloudy / windy / foggy” (adjective), but “It’s raining / snowing” (verb in the present continuous: now). “It rains a lot in Wales” = present simple for a habit.

lignes: It’s sunny. / The sun is shining.
It’s raining. / It rains a lot.

exemples: It’s very windy on the beach today.
It often snows in Quebec in January.

texte: From coldest to hottest: “freezing”, “cold”, “cool”, “warm” (pleasantly hot), “hot”, “boiling” (informal: very hot).
Degrees: “It’s 25 degrees.” / “It’s minus five.” (−5). The UK and Canada use Celsius; the US uses Fahrenheit (25 °C ≈ 77 °F).
Careful: for a person, say “I’m cold” / “I’m hot”, not “I have cold”. And “humid” = hot and heavy, wet air; “wet” = covered in water, rainy.
exemples: It’s freezing this morning! It’s minus three.
It’s about thirty degrees in Yaoundé today.
Can you close the window? I’m cold.

texte: The seasons: “spring”, “summer”, “autumn” (US “fall”), “winter”; “in summer”, “in the winter”. In tropical countries: “the rainy season” and “the dry season”.

Forecasts (“the weather forecast”) use the future: “It’s going to rain this afternoon.” (you can see it coming, lesson 45); “Tomorrow will be sunny.”; “There will be showers in the north.” (short periods of rain).
To react: “I hope it’ll be sunny at the weekend.” “What’s the forecast for tomorrow?”
exemples: Look at those black clouds. It’s going to rain.
The forecast says it will be warm and sunny tomorrow.
In Cameroon, the rainy season starts in March in the south.

texte: British people often start a conversation with the weather, using a question tag (lesson 69): “Lovely day, isn’t it?” “Cold today, isn’t it?” “Terrible weather, isn’t it?”
The expected answer is short and agrees: “Yes, beautiful!” / “Yes, it’s freezing!” / “I know, it hasn’t stopped raining all week.”
Useful expressions: “It’s pouring (down).” / “It’s raining cats and dogs.” (= it’s raining very hard; the second is a bit old-fashioned), “I’m soaked!” (= very wet), “What a lovely day!”
exemples: Lovely weather, isn’t it? — Yes, it’s beautiful!
Cold today, isn’t it? — Yes, it’s freezing!

formule: What’s the weather like? · It’s sunny / cloudy / windy / cold. · It’s raining / snowing. · It’s 20 degrees. · It’s going to rain. · Lovely day, isn’t it?
prononciation: “weather” /ˈweðə/ and “whether” /ˈweðə/ sound the same; the th is voiced /ð/, as in “the”.
“Lovely day, isn’t it?”: falling intonation ↘ on “isn’t it”: it’s not a real question; you expect agreement.
erreurs: It’s nice weather. / The weather is nice.
It’s rainy now, take an umbrella.
It’s raining now, take an umbrella.
It’s sunny today, it doesn’t it?
It’s raining a lot in London in general.
It rains a lot in London.

dialogue.contexte: At a bus stop in Edinburgh, Mrs Reid talks to Léa, a Belgian student who has just arrived.
lignes: Small talk with a question tag.
Yes, it’s freezing! Is it always like this in Scotland?
like this = the same as now.
Not always. It rains a lot, but we have some lovely days in summer.
What’s the weather like in summer?
It’s usually cool, about eighteen degrees. Where are you from?
I’m from Belgium. The weather is similar there, but it’s less windy.
Well, the forecast says it’s going to snow tonight.
Really? I hope it’ll be sunny at the weekend.
Don’t count on it! Ah, here’s my bus. Nice talking to you.
Don’t count on it = it probably won’t happen.

mots: What’s the weather like in Paris?
the sun, rain, wind, etc. at a time and place (uncountable)
It’s cloudy, but it isn’t raining.
It’s too windy to go sailing.
There will be showers this afternoon.
It’s freezing outside, wear a coat.
Have you seen the weather forecast?
what experts say the weather will be
a thing you hold over your head in the rain
I walked home in the rain and I’m soaked.

items: It’s very (snowing / snowy) in the mountains in winter. It snows a lot.
It’s (wind / windy) today. Hold your hat!
It (rains / is raining) a lot in Ireland.
Look at those clouds. It’s ___ to rain.
Have you seen the weather ___ for tomorrow?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: How is the weather like in Brussels?
What’s the weather like in Brussels?
The weather is lovely. / It’s lovely weather.

exercices.consigne: In 5 or 6 sentences, describe today’s weather where you live, the usual weather in each season, and the forecast for tomorrow.
items: Today in Douala it’s hot and humid. It’s about thirty-two degrees and it’s cloudy. It rains a lot here, especially in the rainy season, from March to November. In the dry season it’s sunny and very hot. The forecast says it’s going to rain tomorrow afternoon, so I’ll take my umbrella.

a_retenir: Always the subject “it”: It’s cold. It’s raining. What’s the weather like?
Adjective to describe (sunny, cloudy, windy, foggy); -ing verb for what is happening now (It’s raining / snowing).
“weather” is uncountable: nice weather (not “a nice weather”). A person: I’m cold.
Forecasts: It’s going to rain (evidence); It will be sunny tomorrow.
Small talk: Lovely day, isn’t it? — Yes, beautiful!
